introduction_markdown:
**Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Geography 2 (0750), Paper 2, ADVANCED LEVEL, JUNE 2024. Duration: THREE HOURS.**

Instructions to candidates: Answer FOUR questions, choosing at least ONE from each Section.

All questions carry twenty-five marks each. You are encouraged to refer to specific examples drawn from any part of the world. Credit will be given for such specific examples.

Only the required number of questions will be marked.

Marks will be awarded for well annotated maps and diagrams where these are relevant.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

Les faits cités sont à faire relire par un géographe avant toute mise en avant.

Sujet scanné de cinq pages (page de garde, deux pages de questions, une page de planche de carte topographique 1:50 000 « Dufftown » avec ses signes conventionnels, puis le fond de carte du Cameroun pour la question 3c i). Page de garde vérifiée : ADVANCED LEVEL, Geography, Paper 2, code 0750, JUNE 2024, Three Hours. Filigranes gcerevision.com ignorés. Seul le fond de carte du Cameroun (page 5) est utilisé (question 3).

Points : chaque question est imprimée à 25 marks et les sous-parties somment bien à 25 (Q1 8+8+9, Q2 6+10+9, Q3 8+8+(3+6=9), Q4 6+10+9, Q5 5+9+11, Q6 8+9+8, Q7 EITHER 9+8+8, OR 6+10+9). questions.enonce_markdown:
a) Distinguish between the pedogenic processes of ferrallitisation and calcification.

(8 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Pedogenic processes** are the processes by which soils form. Ferrallitisation (laterisation) and calcification are two major zonal processes, and they differ as follows (4 marks each, with a conclusion).

**1. Ferrallitisation (laterisation).**
- **Climate and location:** hot, wet tropical and equatorial climates with heavy, year-round or long-season rain and high temperatures (the rainforest of the Congo Basin, southern Cameroon, the Amazon, South-East Asia).
- **Process:** intense chemical weathering (hydrolysis) to great depths; the heavy rain percolates **downwards** and **leaches** (washes out) the soluble bases (calcium, magnesium, sodium, potassium) and silica (desilication). What stays behind are insoluble **iron and aluminium sesquioxides** and kaolinite clay.
- **Result:** deep (several metres), red or yellow, acid, clayey **ferralsols** (oxisols) with no clear horizons, low in nutrients and in humus (the litter decomposes and is recycled in the vegetation); low fertility once the forest is cleared; a hard iron crust (laterite or duricrust) may form if the soil dries after clearing.

**2. Calcification.**
- **Climate and location:** semi-arid to sub-humid temperate grasslands (steppes, prairies, the Russian steppe: chernozems), where evaporation is greater than or about equal to rainfall and there is a dry season; also in dry tropical areas.
- **Process:** rain is limited and leaching is weak, so the **calcium carbonate** is not removed from the soil. In the dry season, water is drawn **upwards** by capillary action and evaporation, and carries calcium and other bases; it is deposited as **calcium carbonate** (in nodules or a layer, the Ca horizon) in the lower B horizon, or in the A horizon.
- **Result:** a dark, thick, humus-rich topsoil (from the decay of grass roots), alkaline to neutral (pH greater than 7), with a calcium carbonate layer below; **fertile**, good crumb structure (chernozems and chestnut soils: the world's cereal lands).

**Summary of the distinction:** the main difference is the **direction of water movement and what is left in the soil**: in ferrallitisation downward leaching removes the bases and silica, leaving iron and aluminium oxides (acid, red, infertile); in calcification the weak leaching and upward capillary movement leave calcium carbonate in the profile (alkaline, dark, fertile).

questions.enonce_markdown:
b) Briefly explain why the food chain occurs as a pyramid and state its implication in the sustainability of the ecosystem's equilibrium.

(8 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Why the food chain forms a pyramid (4 marks)**

A food chain shows the flow of energy and matter from **producers** (green plants), which capture solar energy by photosynthesis, to **primary consumers** (herbivores), **secondary consumers** and **tertiary consumers** (carnivores), with the decomposers acting on all levels.

- At each step, only about **10 per cent** of the energy (and so of the biomass) passes from one trophic level to the next. The rest is lost as heat in respiration, used in movement and living processes, lost in excreta, or left in parts that are not eaten (bones, roots, fur) and passed to the decomposers.
- Therefore each level has **less energy, less biomass and, in general, fewer individuals** than the level below it, so the chain, drawn as a diagram with bars, takes the form of a **pyramid** with a broad base of producers and a narrow top of top carnivores. (In a few cases the pyramid of numbers or of biomass can be inverted, for example one large tree supporting many insects, but the pyramid of energy is always a pyramid.)
- For this reason food chains are short (usually 4 or 5 levels), since too little energy remains to support further levels.

**Implications for the sustainability of the equilibrium of the ecosystem (4 marks)**

1. **The base supports everything:** the stability of the ecosystem depends on a broad, healthy base of producers. Anything that destroys or reduces the producers (deforestation, bush burning, pollution, drought) causes the collapse of the upper levels.
2. **Top predators are vulnerable and regulate numbers:** with so few top carnivores, and a small energy supply, they are the first to disappear when the habitat is reduced or when they are hunted (poaching of lions, leopards or eagles). Their loss lets the herbivores multiply and overgraze, which upsets the balance.
3. **Concentration of toxins:** pesticides and heavy metals (DDT, mercury) are not broken down, so their concentration increases at each level (**bioaccumulation and biomagnification**), and the top consumers, including humans, are the most affected; this threatens the survival of species.
4. **Limits to use:** since there is a great loss of energy at each step, the harvest from the ecosystem (fishing, hunting, grazing) must stay within the rate of regeneration of the lower levels, otherwise the equilibrium is lost; for people it is more energy-efficient to eat at a lower level (plants), which supports a higher carrying capacity.

**Conclusion:** sustainable use of an ecosystem requires protecting the producers and biodiversity, controlling harvesting and pollution, and keeping the numbers at each level in balance.

questions.enonce_markdown:
c) (i) On the outline map of Cameroon provided, illustrate the distribution of the major grassland and forest biomes south of the Adamawa Plateau.

![fig-1](gce-al-geography-2024-p2-officiel-cameroun_exercice_3_fig_1.png)

(ii) Account for **TWO** characteristics of the forest biomes identified in c(i) above.

(3 + 6 = 9 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Distribution of the biomes south of the Adamawa Plateau (3 marks)**

On the outline map, the candidate should shade or hatch, label and key the main biomes, which run roughly as **east-west belts** across the south of the country, with the highlands in the west (the model map is schematic and the boundaries are approximate; the outline map to be filled is shown in the question).

![fig-2](gce-al-geography-2024-p2-officiel-cameroun_exercice_3_fig_2.png)

1. **Evergreen equatorial (dense) rainforest** in the south and south-east, to about 4 to 5 degrees north (the Centre, South, East and Littoral regions, and the South-West region: the Congo Basin forest, for example Dja, Campo Ma'an and Korup).
2. **Forest-savanna transition: semi-deciduous forest and derived savanna** to the north of the evergreen forest, between about 4.5 and 6 degrees north, in the Centre (the Mbam and Sanaga areas) and the north of the East region, with patches of grassland within the forest.
3. **Montane forest and grassland** on the Western Highlands (the Bamenda and Bamileke highlands, Mount Oku, Manengouba, Bamboutos, Mount Cameroon): grassland (the grassfields) with remnants of montane forest.
4. **Mangrove swamp forest** in a thin strip along the coast, in the estuaries (the Wouri estuary near Douala, the Rio del Rey and the Ndian area, Kribi).
5. The Adamawa Plateau and the north (savanna and Sahel) are outside the question.

The map should have a **title, a key, and the frame with the latitude and longitude marks** as given (2 to 12 degrees north, 10 to 16 degrees east) and a north point if required.

**(ii) Two characteristics of the forest biomes, with explanation (6 marks: 3 each)**

*Biome chosen: the evergreen equatorial rainforest of southern Cameroon.*

**1. Tall, evergreen, dense trees, arranged in layers (emergent layer, canopy, understorey, shrub and herb layer) with many lianas and epiphytes.**
- *Account:* the climate is hot (mean about 25 to 27 degrees Celsius with very small annual range) and wet (about 1,500 to 4,000 mm with no real dry season), so there is **no season of rest** and plants grow all year, and they are evergreen (leaves are shed and replaced throughout the year; they have drip-tips to shed water). The abundant light and water, and the **intense competition for light**, produce tall trees (30 to 50 m, with emergent trees even taller), a dense closed canopy and several layers, and the climbing plants and epiphytes reach the light. Trees are shallow-rooted and have **buttress roots** to stay upright, since the nutrients are in the upper soil.

**2. Very high biodiversity (many species per hectare, each species represented by few individuals) and rapid nutrient cycling.**
- *Account:* the stable, warm, wet climate has lasted for a very long time, the many layers provide many habitats and niches, and there is plenty of food all year round; so a very large number of species (including timber species such as sapele, iroko and ayous, and many animals such as gorillas, chimpanzees and forest elephants) can exist. The soils are deep but leached and poor in nutrients (ferrallitic), so the nutrients are held mainly in the **biomass**: leaf litter is decomposed within weeks by bacteria, fungi and termites, and the nutrients are taken up at once by the shallow roots; this explains the thin humus layer and why the forest cannot be replaced easily when it is cleared.

(Other characteristics that could be chosen: the evergreen leaves with a waxy surface and drip-tips; the thin bark; the lack of seasonal rhythm of growth; the many climbers and epiphytes; the thick layer of vegetation, with little undergrowth in the shade at ground level; the dense canopy with little light reaching the ground.)
